source.title_on_document: No Evidence for LLMs Being Useful in Problem Reframing

supplement.where: No supplement or data/code repository is mentioned. Footnote 1 (p. 1) links an interactive demo: https://joongishin.github.io/problemReframing_llm/. Appendices A-E are inside this PDF.
supplement.holds: Nothing statistical. The appendices (in this PDF) hold prompts, interfaces, the quiz, the three design problems, the pilot study, and demographics. No arm means, SDs, or test statistics for the main contrasts appear anywhere; the main-text results give box plots and 'all p > 0.05'.

paper_design_summary: Designers recruited on Prolific and CloudResearch were randomly assigned to reframe one of three design problems either without AI (manual) or with GPT-4o in one of three ways: direct generation of frames, a structured nine-step (Dorst) process, or free-form chat in ChatGPT. Each participant submitted two problem frames and the frame they selected as best was rated for novelty and usefulness by 15 high-quiz-score participants acting as expert raters, blind to condition. Agency, ownership, perceived helpfulness (CSI), and effort (NASA-TLX) were self-reported.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Reframing approach (manual without LLM, direct, structured, free-form with GPT-4o) and one of three design problems
assignment.quote: Our study followed a between-subjects design with four levels: (manual, direct, free-form, and structured). Participants were assigned to these conditions in line with balanced Latin square randomization.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 4.1; also p. 5, Section 4 ('We randomly assigned participants to one of the conditions') and p. 6, Figure 4

arms.name: Manual (baseline)
arms.description: Reframe the problem alone, no LLM

arms.name: Direct
arms.description: Button-driven interface in which GPT-4o generates (and regenerates) alternative problem frames from the problem description; participants build on them

arms.name: Structured
arms.description: Button-driven interface in which GPT-4o generates intermediate content for each step of Dorst's nine-step reframing process and then frames; content can be regenerated or added per step

arms.name: Free-form
arms.description: Free conversation with default ChatGPT (GPT-4o) on the participant's own account; conversation log submitted

participants.exclusions: 456 recruited; Figure 4 shows all 456 passing through randomization. 176 removed after assignment: failed attention checks, frames in incorrect format, under 10 minutes on the reframing task, or assigned to an LLM approach but did not use the LLM (the last rule applies only to AI arms). Per-arm exclusions not reported. Final 280: manual 62, direct 72, structured 88, free-form 58 (LLM arms combined 218).
participants.who: People with a design background (product, UI/UX, graphic, game design, architecture, fashion) screened on Prolific and CloudResearch; 76 percent with more than three years of design experience; paid 16 euros, with a 5-euro bonus for the top 10 percent of frames
participants.quote: We recruited 456 individuals by means of the two crowdsourcing platforms. ... We also removed people who were assigned to LLM-based approaches but did not use LLMs. In the end, we had 280 participants
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 4.2; per-arm counts p. 9, Figure 8 (table on right)

ai_tool.how_used: Arms differ. Free-form: open chat in default ChatGPT (GPT-4o). Direct: participants press a button and GPT-4o returns full problem frames (closest to ideas_supplied). Structured: button-driven prompt chain through Dorst's nine steps that returns intermediate content and frames (ideas_supplied/other). In the LLM arms participants could submit frames directly or build on LLM-generated ones. Role coded open_chat for the free-form arm, which is closest to free chatbot use.

task.description: Reframe one of three written design problems (aging delivery drivers, cigarette-butt littering, office lunch-spot preference conflict) into two alternative problem frames using Dorst's template ('If the problem of ... is approached as if ..., then the direction of solutions could be ...'), with an explanation of how each frame helps; then select the most-liked frame in the post-survey.
task.duration: Paid for about one hour; mean time to create two frames 23.25 min (manual), 21.82 (direct), 28.35 (structured), 20.78 (free-form) (p. 8, Section 5)

outcomes.name: Novelty of the problem frame (expert-rated)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 15 participants with 3+ correct answers on the five-item reframing quiz, recruited from the phase-1 sample, rated how novel a perspective each frame introduces relative to the original problem description; questionnaire adapted from Doshi and Hauser. Raters blind to condition. Each rater reviewed 36 frames sampled across 4 approaches x 3 problems x 3 frames. Figure 5 axis runs 1 to 9; the scale and how ratings were aggregated per frame are not stated. Analyzed with Mann-Whitney U (manual vs LLM-all) and Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's Bonferroni post hoc (four approaches).

contrasts.reported: Box plots only; 'there were no statistically significant differences for either, between the manual and the llm-all group but also among all the individual approaches (all p > 0.05)'
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Figure 5 (left panel) and Section 5.2; p. 9, Section 5.2 text

contrasts.reported: Box plots only; Kruskal-Wallis / Dunn's across the four approaches, 'all p > 0.05'
Box plots only; no significant differences 'among all the individual approaches (all p > 0.05)'

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same 15 expert raters and procedure as S1-O1, rating how useful a perspective each frame introduces relative to the original problem description. Figure 5 axis runs 1 to 9; scale and aggregation not stated. Same tests as S1-O1.

contrasts.reported: Box plots only; 'no statistically significant differences for either, between the manual and the llm-all group but also among all the individual approaches (all p > 0.05)'
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Figure 5 (right panel) and Section 5.2; p. 9, Section 5.2 text

participants.quote: Using the same procedure and platforms as for the main study, we recruited 36 people

company_involvement.description: Authors at Aalto University; funding from Research Council of Finland, Finnish Center for Artificial Intelligence, ERC, and Aalto departments (p. 14, Acknowledgments). Free-form arm used participants' own ChatGPT accounts; no company role stated.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned individuals (balanced Latin square) to a no-LLM manual arm or one of three GPT-4o arms (p. 5, Section 4.1); 280 people analyzed (manual 62, LLM arms 218; p. 9, Figure 8); novelty and usefulness of each participant's chosen frame rated by 15 blind expert raters (p. 7, Section 4.4; p. 8, Figure 5). Caveat: 176 of 456 were dropped after assignment, including LLM-arm participants who did not use the LLM, a rule with no counterpart in the manual arm; per-arm attrition is not reported. The pilot S2 (36 people) is below 50 and reports no arm comparison.

one_line_finding: Among 280 designers, frames produced with GPT-4o (direct, structured, or free-form; n = 218) were not rated more novel or useful by expert raters than frames produced without it (n = 62), with all p > 0.05 shown only as box plots (p. 8, Figure 5; pp. 8-9, Section 5.2).
open_questions: Whether 456 is a count at assignment: Figure 4 (p. 6) draws all 456 through 'Randomized', but the text says only 'recruited'. Per-arm randomized counts are not given.
No arm means, SDs, or test statistics for the AI contrasts are printed; extraction would need figure digitizing or author data. Box plots in Figure 5 show medians and quartiles, not means.
How the roughly two expert ratings per frame (15 raters x 36 frames over 280 frames) were combined, and the rating scale, are not stated.

Study-level AI role: arms span open chat (free-form) and button-driven generation of frames (direct, structured); coded open_chat for the free-form arm per the primary-record rule. Review may prefer ideas_supplied or other.
Raters were themselves phase-1 participants (high quiz scorers) who rated other participants' frames.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as outcomes because they are not scored on output: agency and ownership (no significant manual vs LLM differences, p. 9, Section 5.3, Figure 6), Creativity Support Index for LLM arms (direct 64.28, SD 18.90; structured 64.85, SD 20.00; free-form 61.01, SD 17.19; no significant differences; p. 10, Section 5.4, Figure 7), and NASA-TLX (no differences). Moderation by quiz-based expertise (H4): within the LLM conditions, quiz 'experts' (n = 79 across all arms; 61 in LLM arms) produced frames rated 12.54 percent more novel than novices (Z = 2.70, p = 0.01); the free-form gap of 20.84 percent was not significant (Z = 2.31, p = 0.06); no usefulness differences (p. 12, Section 5.5; p. 11, Figure 10). This is an expert-vs-novice comparison within arms, not an AI contrast, so it is not coded as a contrast. Expertise split was balanced across arms, chi2(3, N = 280) = 0.70, p = 0.87 (p. 11). No diversity or similarity outcome is reported. Power analysis targeted medium effects at 95 percent power (p. 8, Section 5.1). Abstract says inexperienced designers perceived lower agency with LLMs. S2 (pilot, Appendix D, p. 25): the authors internally reviewed frame quality to confirm the problems allow low- and high-quality frames (2-3 of 12 frames per problem judged novel or useful); no comparison by condition is reported, so S2 lists no outcomes. S2 per-arm counts are left null; the paper states only 3 participants per problem x approach cell and 12 per problem.
